questions.q: Per this lesson's recap, why was this entire 18-lesson course taught without ever requiring a Salesforce org?
options: Because the course's real subject was never Salesforce specifically -- it was general programming concepts, taught through Apex's syntax as the vehicle, and nearly all of it transfers directly and unchanged into real Apex work
Because Salesforce orgs did not exist when this course was written
Because org access is too expensive for a foundational course
Because Apex cannot actually run inside a real Salesforce org
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that this course's subject was programming itself, not Salesforce, and that the concepts taught are general programming knowledge that happens to transfer directly, unchanged, into real Apex.

questions.q: Which of the following does this lesson name as a genuinely new, Salesforce-specific concept reserved for later courses in this path?
options: Variables and data types
If/else conditional branching
Triggers -- Apex code that runs automatically in response to a database event, rather than being called directly
The difference between a parameter and an argument
questions.explain: The lesson lists triggers, SOQL/DML, governor limits, Salesforce DX/scratch orgs, and Lightning Web Components as the Salesforce-specific layer deliberately left for later courses -- in contrast to variables, data types, and conditionals, which this course already covered as general programming concepts.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say governor limits were only mentioned in passing, with no invented specific numbers given?
options: Because governor limits do not actually exist on the Salesforce platform
Because this course deliberately avoids stating precise figures it has not verified, consistent with this course's policy of not inventing specific numbers
Because governor limits apply only to SOQL, never to Apex
Because governor limits were fully covered in Lesson 9's collections lesson
questions.explain: The lesson frames governor limits as a real, platform-enforced concept worth naming, but deliberately gives no invented numbers here, consistent with this course's broader commitment to not inventing unverified specific figures.

questions.q: What self-check does this lesson recommend before moving on to the next course in this path?
options: Memorizing the entire Apex Developer Guide word for word
Skipping ahead without any self-assessment, since the next course covers everything again from scratch
Immediately signing up for a Salesforce Developer Edition org regardless of confidence level

Honestly checking whether you can read unfamiliar Apex-style code and predict its behavior, spot bugs like off-by-one loop errors or unreachable branches, and write a short method to solve a clearly-stated problem -- all without running the code
questions.explain: The lesson's readiness check specifically asks whether you can read code and predict behavior, spot bugs like off-by-one errors and unreachable branches, and write a short method -- all without running it -- as the honest gauge of readiness.

questions.q: According to the Lab, what should a student do after identifying their least-confident lesson in each chapter?
options: Skip that lesson entirely and move to the next course
Rewrite the entire guide.md for that lesson from scratch
Re-read just that lesson's 'Check yourself' section and attempt to answer it from memory before looking back at the lesson body
Report the lesson as broken to the course administrator
questions.explain: The lesson's Lab instructs students to re-read the specific lesson's Check yourself section and attempt it from memory first, calling this the single most useful thing to do before starting the next course.
